items.title: Tails, Skew, and Symmetry

sections.normalized_html: A tail of a distribution is a part that extends away from the main cluster.
sections.readable_text: A tail of a distribution is a part that extends away from the main cluster.

sections.normalized_html: If the left tail of the distribution is longer than the right tail, then we say that the distribution is left-skewed (or negatively skewed). An example of a left-skewed distribution is shown below.
sections.readable_text: If the left tail of the distribution is longer than the right tail, then we say that the distribution is left-skewed (or negatively skewed). An example of a left-skewed distribution is shown below.
[IMG: /graphics/d338ae8bcea99a0a8a120ca0054735bb]

sections.normalized_html: Similarly, if the right tail of the distribution is longer than the left tail, then we say that the distribution is right-skewed (or positively skewed). An example of a right-skewed distribution is shown below.

sections.normalized_html: If the distribution's tails are the same, we say that the distribution is symmetric. An example of symmetric distribution is shown below.

sections.normalized_html: When a distribution is symmetric, and the corresponding histogram has an odd number of bars, the mean and the median always lie within the central column. So, in the case below, both the mean and median lie between [MATH: 60] and [MATH: 79.]

sections.normalized_html: Finally, for any set of grouped data, the modal class is the class (i.e., group) corresponding to the tallest bar on the histogram. For the histogram below, the modal class is [MATH: 40-59.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A histogram is a visual representation of a frequency table for grouped data.

Content:
For example, consider the data set below:

Content:
[MATH: 55, \: 63, \: 65, \: 68, \: 71, \: 75, \: 82]

Content:
In this data set,

Content:
- there is [MATH: 1] number between [MATH: 50] and [MATH: 59,]
- there are [MATH: 3] numbers between [MATH: 60] and [MATH: 69,]
- there are [MATH: 2] numbers between [MATH: 70] and [MATH: 79,] and
- there is [MATH: 1] number between [MATH: 80] and [MATH: 89.]

Content:
We can organize these results in the following frequency table.

Content:
| Value | Frequency |
| [MATH: 50{-}59] | [MATH: 1] |
| [MATH: 60{-}69] | [MATH: 3] |
| [MATH: 70{-}79] | [MATH: 2] |
| [MATH: 80{-}89] | [MATH: 1] |

Content:
To draw the histogram, we divide a horizontal axis into [MATH: 4] equal subintervals, one for each range of values. Then, on each subinterval, we draw a rectangle whose height is equal to the frequency in the corresponding range.

Content:
The resulting graph is shown below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6b3aef3b43ac2e90a73adbd2a4d6fd89]

---

Item 2 — Example: Filling a Missing Column in a Frequency Table

Example Prompt:
The histogram below shows the height distribution, to the nearest centimeter, of a group of high school baseball players.

[IMG: /graphics/767929c22393f430b33ba0e5a2889980]

The frequency table below represents the same information. From left to right, what is missing from the table?

| Height (cm) | Number of Players |
| [MATH: 161{-}170] | [MATH: 6] |
| [MATH: 000−000] | [MATH: 0] |
| [MATH: 181{-}190] | [MATH: 3] |

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The second column of the histogram tells us that there are [MATH: \color{blue}9] players whose height is in the range of [MATH: {\color{blue}171{-}180} \, \text{cm}.]

[IMG: /graphics/fd51628279f2f3ff12ad34143395302a]

Therefore, the missing parts are [MATH: \color{blue}171{-}180] and [MATH: \color{blue}9.]

| Height (cm) | Number of Players |
| [MATH: 161{-}170] | [MATH: 6] |
| [MATH: 171−180] | [MATH: 9] |
| [MATH: 181{-}190] | [MATH: 3] |

---

From the frequency table:

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The first and second bars correspond to the books that have between [MATH: \color{blue} 150{-}199] and [MATH: \color{blue} 200{-}249] pages, respectively.

The height of the first bar is [MATH: \color{red}15] (halfway between [MATH: 10] and [MATH: 20]) and the second bar has a height of [MATH: \color{red}35] (halfway between [MATH: 30] and [MATH: 40]).

[IMG: /graphics/309193dc4bdaf6fa80bc8b271883b826]

Therefore, Tina has [MATH: {\color{red}15} + {\color{red}35} = 50] books that have at most [MATH: 249] pages.

Item 11 — Tutorial: Tails, Skew, and Symmetry

Content:
A tail of a distribution is a part that extends away from the main cluster.

Content:
If the left tail of the distribution is longer than the right tail, then we say that the distribution is left-skewed (or negatively skewed). An example of a left-skewed distribution is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d338ae8bcea99a0a8a120ca0054735bb]

Content:
Similarly, if the right tail of the distribution is longer than the left tail, then we say that the distribution is right-skewed (or positively skewed). An example of a right-skewed distribution is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1eb20ab324697252e4c47a513a733fad]

Content:
If the distribution's tails are the same, we say that the distribution is symmetric. An example of symmetric distribution is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/969dd025a27ac0b58b910f664487c998]

Content:
For symmetric distributions, the mean and the median always lie in the middle group. So, in this case, we know that the mean and median both lie within the values [MATH: 60] and [MATH: 79.]
